description: Phase 0 of #2228: business-analyst questions over the Acme Reader sample, two products (the Miniflux server and its Python client). Single-product rule questions and multi-product FRD impact questions carry the facts a correct answer states and the sources that support them; ambiguous questions expect a follow-up question and unanswerable ones expect 'the sources don't show this'. Multi-turn questions (#2269) carry the analyst's earlier turns in 'before': the last turn is scored, and 'refersBack' says whether it leans on those turns or is a self-contained control asked mid-conversation.

questions.text: How does the Acme Reader server decide when to check a feed for new articles again?

facts.text: The default scheduler is round robin.
Under round robin a feed is checked again after at least 60 minutes by default (SCHEDULER_ROUND_ROBIN_MIN_INTERVAL).

Under the entry-frequency scheduler the wait is one week divided by the product of the number of articles the feed published in the past week and a factor (1 by default), so a larger factor shortens the wait.
The entry-frequency wait is kept between 5 minutes and 24 hours by default.
A feed that published nothing in the past week is checked at the maximum interval under the entry-frequency scheduler.
A longer delay asked for by the feed itself (its TTL, or the Retry-After, Cache-Control or Expires headers) lengthens the wait.

questions.text: When does the Acme Reader server delete old articles, and which articles are never deleted?

facts.text: Read articles are removed after 60 days by default.
Unread articles are removed after 180 days by default.
Starred (bookmarked) and shared articles are never removed by the cleanup.
A removed article leaves a tombstone so the same article is not imported again on a later refresh.
Setting either number of days to -1 turns that cleanup off.

questions.text: After how many failed refreshes does the Acme Reader server stop checking a feed, and what happens then?

facts.text: By default the server stops polling a feed after 3 parsing errors (POLLING_PARSING_ERROR_LIMIT).
Each failed refresh adds one to the feed's error count and a successful refresh resets it to zero.
Once the limit is reached the user has to refresh the feed manually.
Setting the limit to 0 removes it (unlimited retries).

questions.text: What rules does the Acme Reader server apply to a new user's username and password?

facts.text: A username is required and must not already be taken.
A username may contain only letters, digits and the characters _ - @ and .
A password must be at least 6 characters long.

questions.text: How does the Acme Reader Python client sign in to the server?

facts.text: It signs in either with an API key, sent in the X-Auth-Token header, or with a username and password (HTTP basic authentication).
When both an API key and a username and password are given, the API key is used.
Giving neither an API key nor both a username and password is an error (ValueError).
The README recommends the API key as the preferred method.

questions.text: What does the Acme Reader Python client do when the server answers a request with an error?

facts.text: A 404 raises ResourceNotFound and a 401 raises AccessUnauthorized.
A 403 raises AccessForbidden, a 400 raises BadRequest and a status of 500 or above raises ServerError.
Any other error status raises the base ClientError.
Requests time out after 30 seconds unless another timeout is given.

questions.text: Can two Acme Reader users have the same username, and what stops it?

facts.text: No: the server refuses a new user, or a rename, whose username another user already has.
The database enforces it too: the users table declares the username unique.
Usernames are stored and compared in lower case, so two usernames that differ only in letter case count as the same.

questions.why: Walkthrough run 10, BA Q1 (#2198): the answer cited the file's imports (internal/storage/user.go:13-16) for the insert at :72 and missed the database's unique constraint.

questions.text: What states can an article be in on the Acme Reader server, and what happens to an article when it is deleted?

facts.text: An article is either unread or read.
The removed status is no longer used: a migration recorded every removed article as a tombstone and then deleted it.
Deleting an article deletes its row and records a tombstone, so the same article is not imported again.

questions.why: Walkthrough run 10, BA Q8 (#2198): the answer said the removed status is still used; a later migration (internal/database/migrations.go:1489-1495) dropped it.

questions.text: Can the Acme Reader server already mark every article published before a given date as read, and what uses that today?

facts.text: Yes: the server can already mark every unread article published before a given date as read (MarkAllAsReadBeforeDate).
The Google Reader API uses it: its mark-all-as-read request on the reading list calls it.
The web interface's mark all as read takes no date: it marks every unread article in the globally visible feeds as read.

questions.why: Walkthrough run 10, e-16-5 (#2198): chat said MarkAllAsReadBeforeDate has no callers; the Google Reader handler calls it at internal/googlereader/handler.go:1225, through a receiver.

questions.text: On the Acme Reader server, what does a user see after marking the last page of a feed's unread articles as read, and do the category and unread pages behave the same way?

facts.text: The feed page keeps the page offset it was asked for, so once the last page is marked read it can come back empty.
The category page keeps the offset the same way and has the same problem.
The unread page does not: when the offset is past the number of unread articles it goes back to the first page.

questions.why: Walkthrough run 10, e-16-6 (#2198): chat missed the category page and said showUnreadPage has the same paging bug; it restarts at offset 0 (internal/ui/unread_entries.go:38).

questions.text: Does the Acme Reader server record when a user read an article?

facts.text: No: an article has no field for the time it was read.
Changing an article's status updates its changed_at time, but starring or unstarring it updates changed_at too, so changed_at does not say when it was read.
The reading time shown for an article is an estimate of how many minutes it takes to read, computed from its content; it is not when the article was read.

questions.why: Walkthrough run 10, e-17-2 (#2198): the requirement 'Track reading time with read_at timestamp' was grounded in the reading-time estimate code (internal/reader/readingtime/readingtime.go:16-26), which shares only the words.

questions.text: What does FRD-12 change in the Acme Reader server and in the Python client?

facts.text: FRD-12 has two requirements: FRD-12.1 (API keys can expire) and FRD-12.2 (entries can be filtered by reading time).
In the server, API keys gain an expiry date: the API key model, its storage (creation and listing) and the API key creation handler change.
The server needs a database migration to store the expiry date.
In the server, the API key sign-in lookup must refuse an expired key the way it refuses an unknown one.
In the server, the entries endpoint's filters and the entry query builder gain a reading-time filter.
In the Python client, create_api_key needs a way to pass the expiry date; it sends only a description today.
The Python client needs no code change for the reading-time filter, because get_entries passes its keyword arguments through as query parameters.

questions.text: Does the reading-time filter in FRD-12 need a change to the Python client, or only to the server?

facts.text: Only the server needs a code change; the Python client's get_entries already forwards any keyword argument as a query parameter.
On the server the filter belongs with the entries list filters (configureFilters in the API entry handlers) and the entry query builder.

questions.text: Once FRD-12's expiring API keys are in place, what will a script using the Python client see when its key has expired?

facts.text: FRD-12.1 says an expired key is refused exactly as an unknown key is refused.
The server refuses an unknown API key with HTTP 401 Unauthorized.
The Python client turns a 401 into an AccessUnauthorized exception.

questions.text: Which of our two products checks that a new API key has a description that is not already used, and what does the other product do about it?

facts.text: The server checks it: a description is mandatory and must be unique for the user.
The Python client checks nothing; it sends the description and raises BadRequest when the server answers 400.

questions.text: How does the refresh work?
questions.why: Refresh means the server's scheduled feed polling, a manual refresh of one feed or category, or the Python client's refresh_feed / refresh_all_feeds calls.

questions.why: No referent: the parsing-error limit, the batch size, the entries page limit, the password length or the per-host polling limit.

questions.why: No referent: sessions, archived articles, or API keys (which do not expire today).

questions.text: What happens when it fails?
questions.why: No referent: a feed refresh, a sign-in, an integration call or a client request.

before: Can we make it expire sooner?
questions.text: I meant the login sessions.

facts.text: Login (web) sessions are removed after 30 days by default (CLEANUP_REMOVE_SESSIONS_DAYS); lowering that setting makes them expire sooner.
The session cookie's expiry is set from the same setting.

before: When does the Acme Reader server delete old articles, and which articles are never deleted?
questions.text: How often does that run?

facts.text: The cleanup runs every 24 hours by default.
The interval is set with CLEANUP_FREQUENCY_HOURS, in hours (at least 1).

before: What rules does the Acme Reader server apply to a new user's username and password?
questions.text: And when a user changes them later?

facts.text: A changed password must still be at least 6 characters long.
A changed username must not be empty and must not belong to another user.
The allowed-characters rule for usernames is not checked when a username is changed.

before: How does the Acme Reader Python client sign in to the server?
questions.text: Can I change its request timeout?

facts.text: Yes: the client takes a timeout argument, in seconds, when it is created, and uses it for every request.
The default timeout is 30 seconds.

before: How does the Acme Reader server decide when to check a feed for new articles again?
questions.text: How many feeds does it refresh at a time?

facts.text: Each polling interval (60 minutes by default, POLLING_FREQUENCY) the scheduler picks a batch of at most 100 feeds by default (BATCH_SIZE).
The batch is refreshed by a pool of 16 background workers by default (WORKER_POOL_SIZE).

questions.text: Is there a setting for how long the Acme Reader server waits for a feed's website to respond?

facts.text: HTTP_CLIENT_TIMEOUT sets how long the server waits before it cancels a request to the feed's site.
The default is 20 seconds.

before: What does the Acme Reader Python client do when the server answers a request with an error?
questions.text: Which exception do I get when its API key is wrong?

facts.text: The server answers a wrong API key with 401, which the client raises as AccessUnauthorized.
